name: Among Stars
lines: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. A day there (sunrise to sunrise) lasts 176 Earth days, longer than its year of 88 days.
The hottest planet, about 465 °C at the ground, under thick clouds of sulphuric acid. It turns backwards, so the Sun rises in the west.
Home. The only world we know with life and with liquid water lying open on its surface. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to get here.
The red planet: its dust is rusted iron. Olympus Mons, a volcano three times as high as Everest, stands on it. Robot rovers drive there today.
The largest planet: more than 1,300 Earths would fit inside. The Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than the Earth, raging for at least 350 years.
Its rings are mostly ice, some pieces as small as dust and some as big as houses, and are only about ten metres thick in places. Saturn is light enough to float in a vast bath.
It lies on its side, perhaps knocked over long ago, so each pole has 42 years of sunlight and then 42 years of night. Found by William Herschel in 1781.
The windiest planet: winds of over 2,000 km/h. It was found in 1846 by mathematics before anyone saw it, from the way it pulled on Uranus.
through the great refractor
Saturn is about 1.4 billion km away; its light takes about 80 minutes to reach your eye.
Galileo saw the rings in 1610 but could not make out what they were: he called them Saturn's 'ears'. Christiaan Huygens worked out in 1655 that they are a ring.
The bright dot beside it is Titan, Saturn's largest moon, bigger than the planet Mercury and wrapped in an orange haze.
Jupiter and four moons
the moons Galileo found in January 1610
The four bright dots in a line are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, the 'Galilean moons'. Watch them over a few nights and they change places.
Seeing moons go round another planet helped show that not everything circles the Earth.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than Mercury.
along the line between day and night
The best place to look is the terminator, the line between day and night: the shadows there are long and the craters stand out.
The Moon is about 384,000 km away, and its light, which is sunlight reflected, takes about 1.3 seconds to reach you.
The dark plains are the 'maria' (seas): old lava, not water. Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.
in the Sword of Orion, M42
A cloud of gas and dust about 1,350 light years away, where new stars are being born right now.
On a dark night you can see it with no telescope at all, as a faint fuzzy 'star' in Orion's sword.
The four bright stars at its heart are called the Trapezium.
The Andromeda Galaxy
M31, our nearest large galaxy
A whole galaxy of about a trillion stars, some 2.5 million light years away: the light you see set out before there were humans.
It is the farthest thing most people can see with the naked eye.
Andromeda and our own Milky Way are moving towards each other and will merge in about four or five billion years.
the Seven Sisters, M45
A cluster of young hot blue stars about 440 light years away. Most people can count six or seven with their eyes alone; a telescope shows hundreds.
The blue haze round them is starlight lighting up a cloud of dust they are passing through.
Many peoples have stories about them: in Japan they are called Subaru.
Betelgeuse (top left) is a red supergiant so big it would swallow the orbit of Mars.
The Plough (Big Dipper)
The two end stars of the bowl point to Polaris, the North Star.
A queen on her throne, shaped like a W, opposite the Plough across the pole.
The Southern Cross
The smallest constellation, on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Samoa and Papua New Guinea.
Its red heart is Antares, 'the rival of Mars'.
tonight's show: the constellations
A constellation is a pattern people drew; the stars in it are usually at very different distances from us, and only line up from where we stand.
THE GREAT OBSERVATORY
THE STARFALL CANTEEN
Dr. Amara Osei, astronomer
Dr. Amara Osei, the astronomer who keeps the Great Observatory and its terrace of telescopes among the stars
Look up: that light left some of those stars before there were people on Earth. Try the telescopes on the terrace: each one is set on something wonderful. Saturn first, I always say.
Captain Lena Sørensen, shuttle pilot
Captain Lena Sørensen, a shuttle pilot resting between flights among the stars, who flies the ice from the comet mine
She's a sweet ship. From here you can see the whole Milky Way edge-on: that bright band is the disc of our own galaxy, a hundred thousand light years across.
The shuttle hangar
Kofi Mensah, flight controller
Kofi Mensah, who runs the control tower of the little spaceport Among the Stars
Two flights today: the ice run from the comet and a sightseeing hop round the Earth. No wind up here, so no delays. Only meteors, and we track every one.
Rosa Delgado, shuttle mechanic
Rosa Delgado, who keeps the shuttles flying from the hangar
Heat shield tiles, every one checked by hand before each flight. Coming back into air is the hot part: the air in front of the ship squeezes and heats up to over a thousand degrees.
The start of the Solar System Walk
The Sun holds 99.8% of all the mass in the Solar System.

Here the distances between the planets are true to scale: one step of 8 metres is the distance from the Sun to the Earth (about 150 million km). The planets' sizes are not to scale: at this scale the Earth would be a grain of sand.
Walk east along the path to Neptune, 30 times farther out than the Earth.
times as far from the Sun as the Earth
Mateo Ruiz, guide of the Solar System Walk
Mateo Ruiz, who leads walks down the Solar System Walk and loves showing how empty space really is
The first four planets are all crowded round the Sun, see? Then it's a long walk to Jupiter. And Neptune is right out there by the last lamp. Space is mostly space!
The greenhouse of Starfall
Ama Owusu, mayor of Starfall
the mayor of Starfall, the settlement Among the Stars, who knows every one of its two hundred people
Welcome to Starfall! Seven houses, one greenhouse, one canteen, and the best view in creation. The greenhouse feeds us; the comet gives us water. Ice is water, you know, once you melt it.
Wei Chen, greenhouse keeper
the keeper of the Starfall greenhouse
Tomatoes, beans, lettuces, and two orange trees that think they're in Spain. Plants need light, water, warmth and air: we make all four here.
Isla MacLeod, canteen cook
the cook of the Starfall Canteen
Soup of the day is greenhouse tomato. Bread's fresh. Sit anywhere: people come in from the mine at six and it gets loud.
Dr. Yusuf Haddad, settlement doctor
the doctor of Starfall
Low gravity is lovely, but bones and muscles get lazy without work. Everyone here exercises two hours a day, like real astronauts do.
Nia Brooks, schoolteacher
the teacher of Starfall's little school
Today's lesson: why is the sky black here, even by day? Because there is no air to scatter the sunlight. On Earth, the air turns it blue.
The comet-ice mine
Big Tomas, foreman of the ice mine
Big Tomas, foreman of the comet-ice mine, where a fallen comet is mined for its ice
A comet is a dirty snowball: ice and dust left over from when the planets were made, four and a half billion years ago. We dig the ice, melt it, and that's Starfall's water. Mind the carts!
A shooting star is a grain of dust, often no bigger than sand, burning up as it hits air at tens of kilometres a second.
Meteor showers come on the same nights every year, when the Earth passes through the dust a comet has left behind: the Perseids in August, the Geminids in December.
A meteor that reaches the ground is a meteorite.
Priya Nair, meteor counter
Priya Nair, who counts shooting stars at Meteor Watch every night for a science project
Forty-one so far tonight! Lie back and don't look anywhere in particular: your eyes catch them better from the side.
The chain from Laputa
Gulliver's Travels, Part III (Jonathan Swift, 1726)
High above floats Laputa, the flying island, held up and steered by a great loadstone.
Lemuel Gulliver was drawn up to it on a seat at the end of a chain. The seat waits here. Sit on it, and the island will draw you up.
The whole third voyage is there to play: Laputa, Balnibarbi and its Academy, the island of sorcerers, Luggnagg and its immortals, and Japan.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach the Earth.
The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light years away: its light set out over four years ago.
A light year is how far light goes in a year: about 9.5 trillion km.
Most of the stars you see are bigger and brighter than the Sun; the faint small ones are too dim to see without a telescope.
The Milky Way is our own galaxy, seen from inside: a disc of a few hundred billion stars.
A telescope set on
The seat on the chain from Laputa
sit on it, and be drawn up (Gulliver's Travels, Part III)
⛓️ You sit on the seat; the chain tightens, and the island draws you up by pulleys...
The chain hangs still: the island is not ready to take you up yet.
